summary: Internationalized domain names let Unicode names map into the DNS, but the same name can often be written in more than one way that people see as equivalent. These are often called variants. This informational document discusses variants in second-level names registered in top-level domains and the issues they raise for registries.

eli5.summary: One word can sometimes be spelled several ways that look the same to people. This talks about how name registries should handle those look-alike spellings.

questions: how do domain registries handle unicode variants
what is an idna variant bundle
subtitle: How registries handle internationalized domain names that look the same.

tldr.problem: Internationalized domain names can be written in multiple ways that look the same to humans due to language and writing system conventions, but the DNS treats them as different names. Registries disagree on how to handle these variants.
tldr.mechanism: This document surveys how top-level domains actually handle variant domain names, documenting their policies for blocking, bundling, and provisioning names that may appear equivalent.
tldr.outcome: Registries and domain registrants now have a map of existing variant policies across gTLDs and ccTLDs to inform their own choices.

facts.label: Variant strategies
facts.value: Blocking, bundling, withholding, parallel NS, DNAME

facts.label: Character focus
facts.value: Chinese, Latin, Cyrillic, Japanese, Korean, Arabic

today: RFC 6927 is an Informational document published in May 2013 that provides a snapshot of variant policies as of late 2012. The variant handling landscape continues to evolve, with ICANN and registries still developing consensus on best practices for internationalized domain names.

sections.title: Variants in Internationalized Domain Names
sections.content:
Internationalized Domain Names for Applications (IDNA) lets domain names contain characters from the Unicode repertoire, opening the DNS to names in any language. However, some Unicode characters are considered variants of one another due to language conventions, history, and character design. For example, Chinese writing has reformed, creating multiple representations for what speakers consider the same character. Some Latin-script languages omit accents on capital letters in certain contexts. This creates a fundamental problem: the DNS is case-insensitive but treats variants as completely different names, even when they look the same to native speakers.

There is no single agreed-on definition of what constitutes a variant. Different technical communities and different languages define variants differently. The proper handling of variants has been a topic of extensive debate with little consensus on how to handle them or even which characters are variants of each other.
sections.eli5: In some languages, the same word can be spelled in two different ways that look the same to people who speak that language. The DNS does not know they are the same.

sections.title: Variant Terminology and Approaches
sections.content:
A bundle is a set of domain names where the characters in each position are variants of each other, identified using Language Variant Tables. A name is allocated when sponsorship has been granted; it is active when it appears in the zone. Registries use different strategies: blocking prevents some names in a bundle from being registered at all; withholding allows allocation only under certain conditions, such as when the registrant of one name in the bundle registers the others; parallel NS provisions multiple names with identical name server records so they resolve the same way; and DNAME aliasing uses DNS redirects to provide resolution for bundled names.

Different registries have adopted vastly different approaches based on their language communities, ICANN's guidelines, and operational capacity. Some registries block variants entirely, others activate them in bundles, and some take reactive approaches to variant management.
sections.eli5: Registries can prevent look-alikes from being registered, bundle them together so they work the same way, or let them be separate. Different registries pick different approaches.

sections.title: Generic TLD Variant Policies
sections.content:
Generic TLDs (.COM, .NET, .ORG and others) follow different practices. .COM and .NET have extensive variant policies: they block Chinese variants to prevent confusion, while other languages have no bundling or blocking. .ORG restricts the number of variants a single registration can have for Chinese and Cyrillic. .ASIA activates both applied-for and preferred IDN variants in the zone. .CAT bundles IDNs with their equivalent ASCII names and uses DNAME aliasing. .TEL implements bundling for Chinese with atomic operations on the entire bundle, while blocking variants in Japanese. .INFO blocks variant characters and does not allow width variants in Korean.

Most other generic TLDs either have no internationalized domain names at all (.AERO, .COOP, .JOBS, .PRO, .TRAVEL, .XXX) or have minimal variant policies. The variation in approaches reflects both the technical capabilities of registries and their different interpretations of ICANN's guidelines for internationalized domain names.
sections.eli5: Big registries like .COM block Chinese look-alikes to be safe. Others let them through or group them together. Not all registries allow foreign languages at all.

sections.title: Country Code TLD Practices
sections.content:
Country code TLDs (ccTLDs) also vary widely in their variant policies. Some have published policies while many have not. .CN (China) adds variants into the zone file. .GR (Greece) assigns all variants to the domain owner with name servers pointing to the main form. .BR (Brazil) allows bundling where the same accents or hyphens are variant considerations. .TEL and others in the country-code space use blocking for certain scripts like Japanese.

Many ccTLDs do not publish their variant policies or IDN practices in the IANA registry, making their approaches difficult to determine. Some registries publish policy pages; others publish only as IDN tables in the IANA Repository of IDN Practices. The authors note that many tables in the IANA registry are out of date with broken contact information.
sections.eli5: Different countries handle look-alikes differently. Some group them together, others block them, and some do not say what they do.
